main.text: [III, 222] [col. 428] Chapter 14.
On Dragons.

In Hebrew תנין thannin means two things, namely dragon and sea monster, as if the sea monster were a sea dragon. Indeed תנין is sometimes taken for any serpent whatever, just like נחש. So when the rod of Moses is said to be changed לתנין, into a thannin, Exod. VII, 9., that is, לנחש, into a serpent, as Moses himself explains, Exod. IV, 3. and VII, 15. Thus Nasrius, an Arab writer in the Oxford library, when in his Ὀνειροκριτικοῖς [Oneirokritikois] (book 3, sect. 21, ch. 30) he tells of a certain woman who dreamed that she had given birth to الحية [al-ḥayya], [col. 429] a serpent, and she gave birth to a great and celebrated orator: because the تنين [tinnīn] thannin is double-tongued. It is plain that he used تنين [tinnīn] thannin and حية [ḥayya], that is, serpent, for the same thing. Yet not only for the Hebrews and Syrians but also for the Arabs, תנין thannin is properly a dragon. And, to say nothing of other evidence, this is plain from the paraphrasts, who consistently have תנין for dragon in the book of the Revelation of John. Hence تنين [tinnīn] thannin is defined in the Alcamus as حية عظيمة [ḥayya ʿaẓīma], a great serpent ^{(1)}. And [III, 223] among the Arabs التنين [al-tinnīn], the dragon, is either السماوي [al-samāwī], celestial, or الارضي [al-arḍī], terrestrial, or البحري [al-baḥrī], marine. The celestial one, they say, which in Persian is هستبر [hstbr], is a certain fainter whiteness which occupies six signs and changes place with the planets. The sea dragon, in Greek δράκων θαλάσσιος [drakōn thalassios] (in French vive), is the araneus of Pliny, on which see Avicenna, books 2 and 4 of the Canon. The terrestrial one the same author describes in roughly these words, book 4, Fen 6, treatise 3, ch. 53: The smallest in the species of dragons, as some report, is five cubits; the largest, thirty and more. The eyes are large; on the lower jaw there is a projection like a beard. The teeth are very many. They say that many are found in Nubia and India, but that the Indian ones are larger. The Ionian ones in Asia do not exceed four cubits. The Indian ones, besides being the largest and otherwise of the form we have described, have yellow and black faces, very wide mouths, brows covering the eyes, necks covered with scales. In each jaw there are three teeth (that is, rows of teeth).
[III, 224] We ourselves saw one of this kind which had thick hair on both sides of the neck.

It is worth explaining here in passing the barbarous names of dragons cited in what follows, which are everywhere very corrupt, but far more so in the Latin version than in the source, that is, in the Arabic text. First comes Albedisimon Persin. So the Latin translators. But the Arabic text has اغاذنيمون والسير [aghādhnīmūn wa-al-sīr] agadanimon and alsir, or assir, which Avicenna counts among the kinds of dragons. Unless I am mistaken, the first name is made from the Greek ἀγαθοδαίμων [agathodaimōn], which was a by-name of the dragon. Philo of Byblos in Eusebius, On the Preparation for the Gospel, book 1, ch. 7, after showing that the Phoenicians and Egyptians, on the authority of Taautus, attributed something divine to the nature of dragons and serpents, says: Φοίνικες δὲ αὐτὸ (τὸ ζῶον) ἀγαθὸν δαίμονα καλοῦσιν· ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ Αἰγύπτιοι Κνὴφ ἐπονομάζουσι· [Phoinikes de auto (to zōon) agathon daimona kalousin; homoiōs de kai Aigyptioi Knēph eponomazousi;] This animal the Phoenicians call agathodaemon, and the Egyptians likewise call it Kneph. Lampridius on Heliogabalus: he had Egyptian little dragons at Rome, which they call agathodaemons. Servius on these words of the Poet about the viper,
— — — and terrified it shuns the sky,
Georgics book 3: that is, it delights in houses, as do the ἀγαθοὶ δαίμονες [agathoi daimones], whom in Latin they call Genii. Alluding to this, Lucan said of dragons, book 9:
You too, harmless deities to all lands.

And there are the Sir and Isidore's Sirena (or rather Siren): Sirens, he says, are winged serpents in Arabia. And Eucherius: Sirens in Isaiah are demons, or great dragons, crested and also flying. And much earlier Jerome on Esa. XIII, 22.: But the Sirens are called תנין; these we have rendered either demons, or certain monsters, or at any rate great dragons, which are crested and flying. They would better have said Sirenes, whom the poets describe very differently. But for the Fathers the Siren is a species of dragon, [col. 430] because in the Greek version it occurs several times for תנין: as in Iob. XXX, 29. Esa. XXXIV, 13. and XLIII, 20. From this, then, the Arabic سير [sīr] sir for dragon was formed.
There follows the chapter On the bite of the sea dragon, where he means not the araneus but the sea scorpion of Aetius, as will be plain to anyone who compares them.

There follows a chapter whose title in Latin is De haren carmen, but in Arabic في حيوانان بحريان [fī ḥayawānān baḥriyyān], On sea serpents. And what is meant is σμύραινα [smyraina], muraenae [morays], which the same author calls سوريا [sūriyā]. But the Latin translator here has semurion, and thinks that a doctor was so named, although σμύραινα [smyraina] is a fish. That my conjecture is correct will be plain to those who compare Aëtius with Avicenna. For there Avicenna reproduces the very words of Aëtius about the moray fish.

[III, 225] The title of the following chapter is De Alhatraf et Hauden, which again they hold to be among the kinds of dragons. But in the Arabic there is طروغورون [ṭrūghūrūn] truguron, for which read طروغون [ṭrūghūn], τρύγων [trygōn], that is, the sea stingray; that this is the subject is apparent from a comparison of the same Aëtius with Avicenna. So much for the benefit of the lovers of Arabic. Now from the digression back to the road.

Dragons differ from serpents chiefly in bulk. Accordingly, as we said, the dragon is defined in Alcamus as حية عظيمة [ḥayya ʿaẓīma], a great serpent. And well known is the proverb of the Greeks, Ὄφις, εἰ μὴ φάγῃ ὄφιν, δράκων οὐ γενήσεται [Ophis, ei mē phagē ophin, drakōn ou genēsetai]· A serpent, unless it has eaten a serpent, will not become a dragon. Nor without reason does Augustine say on Psalm. CXLVIII.: Dragons are certain great animals; there are none greater upon the earth. But no one could easily say how large they grow, since here the ancients tell many fables, and nowhere is there greater licence for lying, as we shall now show step by step. Pliny, book 8, ch. 13, reports from Juba that among the Asachaean Ethiopians crested dragons of twenty cubits are bred. Aëtius and Avicenna write that they grow from five cubits up to thirty. This is confirmed from elsewhere too. For in Aelian, History book 2, chapter 21, dragons in Phrygia grow to ten orgyiae; and that each of these is three cubits, Hesychius and Eustathius teach. And Pausanias in the Corinthiaca relates that τοὺς ὄφεις τοὺς Μεγαλαύνας [tous opheis tous Megalaunas], the Megalaunian serpents around Epidaurus grow beyond a size of thirty cubits; such as are said to be bred in India and in Africa. So Philostratus, book 3, ch. 2, where he treats of the species of dragons in India: Οἱ μὲν δὴ ἕλειοι νωθροί τέ εἰσι, καὶ τριακοντάπηχυ μῆκος ἔχουσι [Hoi men dē heleioi nōthroi te eisi, kai triakontapēchy mēkos echousi]· The marsh ones are sluggish, and thirty cubits long. The same was the measure of the Egyptian dragon that was brought alive to Alexandria to Ptolemy Philadelphus. For Tzetzes is mistaken, who makes it τριακονταπεντάπηχυν [triakontapentapēchyn], of thirty-five cubits, Chiliad 3, History 113, since the author he follows, Diodorus, book 3, asserts in express words that it was only τριάκοντα πηχῶν [triakonta pēchōn], of thirty cubits. That he saw one such, Agatharchides, book 5, ch. 41, testifies in these words: Τῶν μέν τοι ὑπὸ τὴν ἡμετέραν ὄψιν πεπτωκότων ὁ μέγιστος, πέφηνε πηχῶν τριάκοντα [Tōn men toi hypo tēn hēmeteran opsin peptōkotōn ho megistos, pephēne pēchōn triakonta]· The largest of those that came under our eyes appeared to be thirty cubits. And in Strabo, book 16: δρακόντων εἴρηκε μεγέθη τριάκοντα πηχῶν ὁ Ἀρτεμίδωρος, ἐλέφαντας καὶ ταύρους χειρουμένων [drakontōn eirēke megethē triakonta pēchōn ho Artemidōros, elephantas kai taurous cheiroumenōn], Artemidorus describes dragons of thirty cubits, which overpower bulls and elephants. I am willing, therefore, that what so many of the ancients attest be held true: that dragons in the bulk of their body reach a measure of thirty cubits [col. 431] or, what is the same, forty-five feet. But most of what follows surpasses belief. In the Periplus of the Red Sea, in Aelian, book 17, ch. 1, Alexander reports that he saw serpents forty cubits in length, to which their breadth and thickness corresponded in proportion. [III, 226] Philostorgius, book 3, ch. 11, mentions dragons in the East and the South, πάχος μὲν δοκῶν οὐκ ἐλάττους, τὸ δὲ μῆκος εἰς δέκα πέντε παρατεινόμενον ὀργυίας [pachos men dokōn ouk elattous, to de mēkos eis deka pente parateinomenon orgyias], not smaller than beams in thickness, and extending in length to fifteen orgyiae (that is, 45 cubits), whose skins, brought to Rome, he himself saw. Suetonius, ch. 43, relates that Augustus exhibited a snake of fifty cubits before the comitium. And under the same emperor Dio, book 50, mentions Τοῦ δικεφάλου δράκοντος τοῦ ἐν τῇ Τυρσηνίδι φανέντος, καὶ ἐς πέντε καὶ ὀγδοήκοντα πόδας ἐξικνουμένου, πολλά τε κακώσαντος, εἶτα κεραυνωθέντος [Tou dikephalou drakontos tou en tē Tyrsēnidi phanentos, kai es pente kai ogdoēkonta podas exikneoumenou, polla te kakōsantos, eita keraunōthentos], a two-headed dragon seen in Etruria, eighty-five feet long, which, after it had laid waste much, was struck by lightning. Of the same kind is what Posidonius in Strabo, book 16, relates of the plain of Coele-Syria, Macra: τὸν δράκοντα πεπτωκότα ὁραθῆναι νεκρὸν, μῆκος σχεδόν τι καὶ πλεθριαῖον, πάχος δ᾽, ὥς θ᾽ ἱππέας ἑκατέρωθεν παραστάντας ἀλλήλους μὴ καθορᾷν, χάσμα δὲ ὥς τ᾽ ἔφιππον δέξασθαι, τῆς δὲ φολίδος λεπίδα ἑκάστην ὑπεραίρουσαν θυρεοῦ [ton drakonta peptōkota horathēnai nekron, mēkos schedon ti kai plethriaion, pachos d᾽, hōs th᾽ hippeas hekaterōthen parastantas allēlous mē kathoran, chasma de hōs t᾽ ephippon dexasthai, tēs de pholidos lepida hekastēn hyperairousan thyreou], that a dead dragon was seen, a plethrum (or a hundred feet) in length, and of such thickness that horsemen standing on either side could not see one another; and with a gaping mouth so wide that it could take in a man sitting on a horse; and finally, each scale of whose skin was larger than a shield. Now what is better known than the dragon of one hundred and twenty feet which Regulus is said to have found lurking by the river Bagradas, not far from Utica? When it was attacked in vain with missiles and javelins by the whole army, it was at last overcome with ballistae and siege engines, like some town. And its skin and jaws lasted in a temple at Rome until the Numantine war. Many writers attest this. But see especially Tubero in Gellius, book 6, ch. 3, Livy in Valerius, book 1, at the end, Pliny, book 8, ch. 14, and Orosius, book 4, ch. 8. What of the fact that Ethiopian and Indian dragons are read not only to equal so portentous a bulk but even to surpass it? For to the Ethiopian ones Aelian, Hist. book 2, ch. 21, ^{(2)}, assigns a length of thirty orgyiae, that is, ninety cubits, or 135 feet. And in the same country there were those who openly asserted that they had seen dragons a hundred cubits long, that is, a hundred and fifty feet; but that their credit is suspect, Diodorus, book 3, testifies in these words: Those who inhabit the region (of Ethiopia) near the desert and full of wild beasts say that many kinds of serpents, incredible in size, are seen. Ἑκατὸν γὰρ πηχῶν τὸ μῆκος ἑωρακέναι τινὲς ἀποφαινόμενοι, δικαίως ἂν οὐχ᾽ ὑφ᾽ ἡμῶν μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὑπὸ τῶν ἄλλων ἁπάντων ψευδολογεῖν ὑπολεφθείησαν [Hekaton gar pēchōn to mēkos heōrakenai tines apophainomenoi, dikaiōs an ouch᾽ hyph᾽ hēmōn monon, alla kai hypo tōn allōn hapantōn pseudologein hypolephtheiēsan], for some, declaring that they have seen them a hundred cubits long, are justly suspected of lying, not only by us but by all others too. As for the Indian ones, Aelian, [III, 227] book 15, ch. 21, mentions one seventy cubits long, or a hundred and five feet, with eyes like a Macedonian shield, worshipped by the Indians with the greatest reverence in a certain cave, which by its breath and hissing alone terrified and threw into confusion the whole army of Alexander. But, as if this were too little, in the same author, book 16, ch. 39, Onesicritus relates that Aposisares the Indian kept two dragons, of which the smaller was eighty cubits, that is, a hundred and twenty feet, the larger a hundred and forty cubits, that is, two hundred and ten feet, which Alexander greatly desired to see. The same you may read in Tzetzes, Chiliad 3, History 113. But Strabo, who writes Biasarus or Abiosarus instead of Aposisares, thus undermines the credit of this fiction: Ἐν τοῖς ὄρεσιν ἡ τοῦ Βιασάρου (MSS. Ἀβιοσάρου) χώρα, παρ᾽ ᾧ δύο δράκοντας ἀπήγγελον οἱ παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ πρέσβεις τρέφεσθαι, [col. 432] τὸν μὲν ὀγδοήκοντα πηχῶν, τὸν δὲ τετταράκοντα πρὸς τοῖς ἑκατὸν, ὡς εἴρηκεν Ὀνησίκριτος, ὃν ἐκ Ἀλεξάνδρου μᾶλλον ἢ τῶν παραδόξων Ἀλεξάνδρου ἀρχικυβερνήτην προσείποι τις ἄν [En tois oresin hē tou Biasarou (MSS. Abiosarou) chōra, par᾽ hō dyo drakontas apēngelon hoi par᾽ autou presbeis trephesthai, ton men ogdoēkonta pēchōn, ton de tettarakonta pros tois hekaton, hōs eirēken Onēsikritos, hon ek Alexandrou mallon ē tōn paradoxōn Alexandrou archikybernētēn prosei pois an]· In the mountains is the country of Biasarus (or Abiosarus), with whom, as the envoys sent by him reported, two dragons were kept, one of eighty, the other of a hundred and forty cubits, on the authority of Onesicritus, whom one might justly call the chief pilot not so much of Alexander's ship as of incredible tales. Yet this is not yet the end of the lies. For these may seem trifles compared with the report that Taxiles, a king neighbouring Abiosarus, showed Alexander a dragon of five plethra, that is, five hundred feet. So Maximus of Tyre, Oration 38: Ἔδειξε καὶ ζῶον ὑπερφυὲς, Διονύσου ἄγαλμα, ᾧ Ἰνδοὶ ἔθυον, δράκων ἦν μῆκος πεντάπλεθρον [Edeixe kai zōon hyperphyes, Dionysou agalma, hō Indoi ethyon, drakōn ēn mēkos pentaplethron], He showed a certain immense animal, an image of Bacchus, to which the Indians sacrificed, namely a dragon five plethra in length. Meanwhile the Greeks are far more modest than the Arabs, one of whom, in Damiri, asserts that he saw تنينا طوله نحو فرسخين ولونه مثل لون النمر مفلسا مثل فلوس السمك بجناحين عظيمين علي هية جناح السمك وراسها كراس الانسان لكنها كالتل العظيم [tinnīnan ṭūluhu naḥwa farsakhayn wa-lawnuhu mithl lawn al-namir mufallasan mithl fulūs al-samak bi-janāḥayn ʿaẓīmayn ʿalī hya janāḥ al-samak wa-rāsuhā ka-rās al-insān lākinnahā kal-tall al-ʿaẓīm] a dragon nearly two parasangs long (that is, eight thousand paces), of the colour of a leopard, scaled with the scales of a fish, furnished also with great fins, like fishes, and having a human head the size of a lofty hill.

There is also much doubt about the form of dragons. For many attribute feet, crests and wings to them. About feet, Paulus Iovius says in book 18: The inhabitants of the Georgian kingdom assert that in these valleys there are winged dragons which creep step by step along the ground on goose-like feet. And Scaliger in Gesner: All kinds of dragons have feet. And again: That dragons have legs is well known. In Pliny, Juba also describes crested ones. And Ovid, Metamorphoses book 4, Fable 15:
[III, 228] They stroke the slippery neck of the crested dragon.
And in book 7, of the dragon that guarded the golden fleece:
Conspicuous for its crest and three tongues. — —

And Philostratus, book 3, ch. 2: Τὸν ἐν τῷ τῆς Νεμέας ἄλσει (δράκοντα) φασὶ καὶ λοφιὰν ἔχειν. Ὅπερ οὐκ ἂν περὶ τοὺς ἑλείους εὕροιμεν· [Ton en tō tēs Nemeas alsei (drakonta) phasi kai lophian echein. Hoper ouk an peri tous heleious heuroimen] They say that the dragon in the grove of Nemea is crested, which we do not find in the marsh dragons. And the same of the mountain dragons: Τούτοις καὶ λοφιὰ φύεται· νέοις μὲν ὑπανίσχουσα τὸ μέτριον, τελειουμένοις δὲ συναυξανομένη τε, καὶ συνανιοῦσα εἰς πολύ. [Toutois kai lophia phyetai; neois men hypanischousa to metrion, teleioumenois de synauxanomenē te, kai synaniousa eis poly.] These too grow a crest; in the young it is moderately raised, but in those advanced in age it is larger and much relaxed. And below: Ἀπὸ δὲ τῶν λόφων, πυρσῶν ὄντων, πῦρ αὐτοῖς ἄττει λαμπάδος πλέον· [Apo de tōn lophōn, pyrsōn ontōn, pyr autois attei lampados pleon] And from their crests, which are red, fire sparkles more than from a torch. And Aelian, book 11, ch. 26: Ὁ μὲν δράκων ὁ ἄῤῥην τὸν λόφον (ἔχει) καὶ τὴν ὑπήνην δασεῖαν· [Ho men drakōn ho arrhēn ton lophon (echei) kai tēn hypēnēn daseian] The male dragon has a crest and a thick beard. And Jerome on Es. XIII.: תנין we have rendered as great dragons, which are crested and flying. And Isidore, Etymologies book 12, ch. 4: And (the dragon) is crested, with a small mouth, etc. Finally, most people think dragons are winged. Lucan, book 9, line 732:
— — — you draw the high air with your wings. — —

Jerome, just cited: They are crested and flying. Augustine, On Genesis Literally, book 3, chapter 9: Dragons, however, etc. are said to be lifted up into the air. [col. 433] And on Psalm CXLVIII: They come forth from caves and are borne into the air. Iovius, as above: The inhabitants of the Georgian kingdom assert that winged dragons are born in these valleys. Scaliger too: Some kinds of dragons have wings. This opinion might seem to be supported by the fact that in Apoc. XII, 7 the mystical dragon fights with Michael in heaven, that is, in the highest air, as though carried up there by wings.

Yet I do not think there is any truth in this description of dragons. For, to begin with the feet, there is no ancient writer who attributes feet to the dragon. And Augustine, in the passage we just cited, expressly teaches that it is ἄπους [apous, footless]. Dragons, he says, without feet, are said both to rest in caves and to be lifted up into the air. Nor are they said to walk, but to creep, in these lines of Lucan:
You too, dragons, divinities harmless to all lands, who creep along shining with golden gleam.

For the dragon is a kind of serpent, which God commanded to creep upon its belly, Gen. III, 14. Now about the crests, Pliny, book 11, chapter 37: No one is found who has seen [III, 229] the crests of dragons. And book 8, chapter 13: This alone is strange: whence Juba came to believe in crested dragons. Finally, no one will easily persuade himself that so vast a mass is raised aloft by wings, and cartilaginous ones at that. Especially since neither the philosophers nor trustworthy historians report anything of the kind. For as to what they say, that in book 16 of Strabo wings are attributed to Indian and Libyan dragons, that is indeed found in Xylander's version, but in the Greek text it is something quite different. It is said not that πτερὰ [ptera], wings, but that πόα ἐπιφυκέναι [poa epiphykenai], grass grows upon them. This seems taken from Iphicrates, who, in book 17 of the same Strabo, speaks of δράκοντας μεγάλους, ὥστε καὶ πόαν ἐπιφυκέναι [drakontas megalous, hōste kai poan epiphykenai] in western Ethiopia, describing dragons so vast that grass grows on them. Nor is an argument from the mystical dragon to the natural one valid. And in fact that mystical dragon itself is nowhere read to have wings. Indeed, you may infer that it is ἄπτερος [apteros, wingless] from the fact that it does not pursue the woman who flies away on eagle's wings, but, doing the one thing it can, spews a flood of water after her, Apoc. XII, 14. 15. So too in the fight of the eagle with the dragon in Nicander's Theriaca, when the eagle escapes the danger by flight,
— — ἱπτάμενον δὲ πέριξ ἀτέλεστα διώκει Σπειρηθεὶς, καὶ λοξὸν ὑποδρὰξ ὄμμασι λεύσσων, [— — hiptamenon de perix atelesta diōkei Speirētheis, kai loxon hypodrax ommasi leussōn,]
it (the dragon) pursues it in vain as it flies round about, coiled in spirals, glaring at it with sidelong and grim eyes. For it cannot reach the eagle once it has risen on high.
Therefore I do not see where this popular opinion that dragons are winged came from, unless we trace it to the mythographers and poets, who, together with painters,
have always had an equal licence to dare anything.
Drawing on this, then, they have the chariot of Ceres drawn by winged dragons. Orpheus in the Hymn to Ceres:
Ἅρμα δρακοντείοισιν ὑποζεύξασα χαλινοῖς, [Harma drakonteioisin hypozeuxasa chalinois,]
Yoking the reins of (winged) dragons to the chariot. Ovid, Metamorphoses book 5, Fable 11:
— — The fertile goddess set twin snakes to her chariot, curbed their mouths with reins, and was borne through the air between heaven and earth.
And in book 4 of the Fasti:
— — she yoked bridled snakes to her chariot, and dry-shod wanders over the waters of the sea.
And below, [III, 230] — — — and she passes over to the dragons, and Ceres is raised aloft on the winged axle.
Claudian, book 1 On the Rape of Proserpina:
— — — guiding the sinuous limbs of dragons, which mark the clouds, passable to them, with their winged course [col. 434] and moisten the reins with gentle poison.
Borne in this very chariot into Scythia, Triptolemus said to Lyncus, king of Scythia, in Ovid at the place cited above:
— — — I came neither by ship over the waves, nor on foot over the lands: the open air lay passable before me.
That is, of Ceres
Δίφρον ἐχιδνήεντα δι᾽ ἠέρος ἡνιοχεύων, Στικτὰ φερεσταχύων ἐπεμάστιε νῶτα δρακόντων, [Diphron echidnēenta di᾽ ēeros hēniocheuōn, Stikta pherestachyōn epemastie nōta drakontōn,]

Driving the chariot through the air, he lashed the spotted backs of the ear-bearing dragons. So Nonnus, book 13 of the Dionysiaca. For Ceres sent him, borne by winged dragons, through the whole world to show men the use of grain. So teach Hyginus, Fable 147, and book 2 of the Astronomica, on Ophiuchus; Servius on book 1 of the Georgics; Phornutus in the book On the Nature of the Gods, chapter On Ceres; and not a few others. To say nothing of Medea, whom they feign to have received such a chariot from her father, the Sun. The Scholiast on Euripides in the Argument of the Medea: Μήδεια δὲ, τοὺς ἑαυτῆς παῖδας ἀποκτείνασα, ἐφ᾽ ἅρματος δρακόντων πτερωτῶν ἔποχος γενομένη, ἀποδιδράσκει εἰς Ἀθήνας [Mēdeia de, tous heautēs paidas apokteinasa, eph᾽ harmatos drakontōn pterōtōn epochos genomenē, apodidraskei eis Athēnas]. This is taken from Apollodorus at the end of book 1 of the Bibliotheca. Hence of the same woman Ovid, Metamorphoses book 7, Fable 2:

Not in vain: a chariot drawn by the necks of winged dragons is there; the chariot had come down from the sky. As soon as she mounted it and stroked the bridled necks of the dragons, and shook the light reins with her hands, she is swept on high. — — —
And Fable 5:
Had she not gone into the air on winged serpents, she would not have escaped punishment. — — —
And Fable 20:
At last on viperine wings she reached Ephyraean Pirene. — — — [III, 231] And Fable 21:
Carried off from here by Titanian dragons, she enters the Palladian citadel. — — —

Nor is it surprising that Circe is sometimes borne in this same chariot, since she too was a daughter of the Sun and the sister of Medea. Accordingly in Apollonius (Argonautica book 3, line 308) Circe is brought to Hesperia, that is Italy,
— — πατρὸς ἐν ἅρμασιν Ἡελίοιο, [patros en harmasin Ēelioio,]
in the chariot of her father, the Sun. The excellent Scholiast reports that he has this from Hesiod. And Valerius Flaccus, book 7:
— — as the winged dragons carried off Circe.
And below in the same place:
— — — was Circe at last scarcely restored, harsh to your people, whom flight drove hence with a pair of serpents? — — —

But that ships are signified by the name of dragons is taught by those very ancients: as in Eusebius' Chronicle the most celebrated writer Philochorus, when he reports that under Celeus, king of Eleusis, Triptolemus μακρῷ πλοίῳ προβαλόντα ταῖς πόλεσι τὸν σῖτον διαδοῦναι· ὑπονοεῖσθαι δὲ πτερωτὸν ὄφιν εἶναι τὴν ναῦν, ἔχειν δέ τι καὶ τοῦ σχήματος [makrō ploiō probalonta tais polesi ton siton diadounai; hyponoeisthai de pterōton ophin einai tēn naun, echein de ti kai tou schēmatos], having been carried in a long ship, distributed grain to the cities; and that the ship is signified by the winged serpent, since its shape is in some respect similar. Add, if you like, that a ship could be marked with the name Dragon which had a dragon as its ensign: as in Plutarch, in the book On the Virtues of Women, the pirate Chimarrus, slain by Bellerophon, ἔπλει πλοίῳ λέοντα μὲν ἔχοντι πρώραθεν ἐπίσημον, ἐκ δὲ πρύμνης δράκοντα [eplei ploiō leonta men echonti prōrathen episēmon, ek de prymnēs drakonta], sailed in a ship that had a lion on the prow and a dragon on the stern as its ensign. And in Euripides, Iphigenia in Aulis, the Boeotian ships had as their sign Cadmus
Χρύσεον δράκοντ᾽ ἔχων Ἀμφὶ ναῶν κόρυμβα· [Chryseon drakont᾽ echōn Amphi naōn korymba;]

holding a golden dragon on the beaks of the ships. To the same point belongs the fact that in the Fables [col. 435] those who are borne by dragons set out only from coastal places and only to coastal places. Thus Ceres, seeking Proserpina, after she had travelled over all Sicily without dragons, at last came also to the shores of the island:

As soon as she arrived there, she yoked bridled snakes to her chariot, and roams dry over the waters of the sea. [III, 232] So Ovid in book 4 of the Fasti. And Circe is carried from Colchis in a chariot of dragons to the promontory Circeium in Italy; Medea, after slaying her children, from Corinth to Athens; Triptolemus from Athens to Patrae, a coastal city of Achaea, where the son of Eumelus, Antheas, who dared to yoke dragons after the example of Triptolemus, was thrown from the chariot and perished; that is, he suffered shipwreck, having attempted the sea without skill in navigation. The story is found in the Achaica of Pausanias. But we argue in vain, since it is the part of a Coroebus or a Margites (that is, of fools) to believe Τριπτόλεμον ἐλάσαι διὰ τοῦ ἀέρος ἐπὶ δρακόντων ὑποπτέρων [Triptolemon elasai dia tou aeros epi drakontōn hypopterōn], that Triptolemus was carried through the air by winged dragons, as Lucian rightly asserts in the Philopseudes, mocking these fictions of the poets. In the same spirit Augustine, or whoever is the author of the book, in the Soliloquies, book 2, chapter 15: For when it is said that Medea flew with winged snakes yoked together, that thing in no respect imitates the truth; for it is nothing, and a thing that does not exist at all cannot imitate anything. Yet wings grew on dragons from no other source than fictions of this kind.

But other marks are not lacking by which dragons are distinguished from the common run of serpents. Among these let the first be vast bulk, as frequent in dragons as it is rare and unusual in other serpents. The second, a beard and dewlaps under the chin. Nicander,
— — — νέρθε δὲ πώγων Ἔπλεθ' ὑπ' ἀνθερεῶνα χολοίβαφος, [— — — nerthe de pōgōn Epleth' hyp' anthereōna choloibaphos,]

But below, under the chin, is a yellow beard. Aelian, book 11, chapter 26: Ἔχει γοῦν ὁ μὲν δράκων ὁ ἄῤῥην τὸν λόφον, καὶ τὴν ὑπήνην δασεῖαν· [Echei goun ho men drakōn ho arrhēn ton lophon, kai tēn hypēnēn daseian;] The male dragon indeed has a crest and a shaggy beard. Avicenna: وتحت الفك الاسفل نتو كالذقن [wa-taḥt al-fakk al-asfal nutūʾ ka-l-dhaqan] And under the lower jaw (they have) a protuberance like a beard. Philostratus does not attribute a beard to all, but to a certain kind of dragons: Οἵδε δὴ πυρσῖται, he says, καὶ περιόνωτοι γίνονται, οὗτοι καὶ γενειάσκουσι· [Hoide dē pyrsitai … kai perionōtoi ginontai, houtoi kai geneiaskousi;] Those that have a fiery colour and a serrated back also grow a beard. The third, a triple row of teeth, if indeed Nicander is right,
— — — ἐν δὲ γενείῳ Τρίστιχοι ἑκάτερθε περιστιχόωσιν ὀδόντες, [— — — en de geneiō Tristichoi hekaterthe peristichoōsin odontes,]

And in the jaw three rows of teeth are ranged on either side. Avicenna has only وفي كل لحي ثلثة انياب [wa-fī kull laḥy thalātha anyāb] And in each jaw there are three teeth. But I think something has been omitted, namely the word صفوف [ṣufūf] or سطور [suṭūr], that is, rows. Let the fourth mark be colour, which is indeed varied. For Aëtius observes that some are black, some red, some ash-coloured. And, according to Avicenna, [III, 233] لها وجوه صفر وسود [lahā wujūh ṣufr wa-sūd] Their faces are yellow and black. And long before, Nicander,
Φράζεο καὶ χλοάοντα δαεὶς κύανόν τε δράκοντα, [Phrazeo kai chloaonta daeis kyanon te drakonta,]
Being skilled, describe also the yellow and the black dragon. Yet they are mostly described as tawny, or yellow, or golden, or red in colour, which is nearly the same thing. Lucan,
You dragons, gleaming with golden brightness, crawl.

Pausanias in the Corinthiaca: Δράκοντες δὲ οἱ λοιποὶ, καὶ ἕτερον γένος, ἐς τὸ ξανθότερον ῥέποντες χρόας, ἱεροὶ μὲν τοῦ Ἀσκληπιοῦ νομίζονται· [Drakontes de hoi loipoi, kai heteron genos, es to xanthoteron rhepontes chroas, hieroi men tou Asklēpiou nomizontai;] The other [col. 436] dragons also, but (especially) another kind, inclining to a tawny colour, are held sacred to Aesculapius. And Philostratus, in the place cited above, after saying that πυρσίτας [pyrsitas] (that is, fire-coloured) dragons have a serrated back and are bearded, adds: καὶ τὸν αὐχένα ὑψοῦ αἴρουσι, καὶ τὴν φολίδα στίλβουσι δίκην ἀργύρου [kai ton auchena hypsou airousi, kai tēn pholida stilbousi dikēn argyrou], and they raise the neck higher, and their scales shine like silver: so that he teaches that these stand out most among dragons. Thus the supreme Poet did not write in vain, Iliad 2, line 308:
Ἔνθ᾽ ἐφάνη μέγα σῆμα, δράκων ἐπὶ νῶτα δαφοινός· [Enth' ephanē mega sēma, drakōn epi nōta daphoinos;]

There appeared a great sign, a dragon red on the back (or ruddy). Not much differently the divine writer, Apoc. XII, 1. 3. A great sign appeared in heaven, etc. And behold a great red dragon! Although something else is signified: namely the devil, who is bloodthirsty and a murderer from the beginning, Ioh. VIII, 44, and inflamed with wrath, and burning, because his time is short, Apoc. XII, 12. With this in view the Syriac translator renders ܬܢܝܢܐ ܕܢܘܪܐ, a fiery dragon. And the Arabic: تنين بلون النار [tinnīn bi-lawn al-nār] a dragon of fiery colour. Which is in Philostratus πυρσίτης [pyrsitēs], and in John πυῤῥὸς [pyrrhos], that is, πυρόεις τὴν χροιάν [pyroeis tēn chroian].

Some describe the gape of the dragon as small, others as large. Solinus was of the former opinion: he says that dragons have small mouths, which do not open wide to bite, so that they do harm by a blow rather than by their gape. Isidore follows him: It has, he says, a small mouth and narrow pipes, through which it draws breath and puts out its tongue. Its strength, however, lies not in its teeth but in its tail, and it does harm by a blow rather than by its gape. But Aëtius says the contrary: They have a very wide gape of the mouth. And Avicenna, who had seen them: لها افواه شديدة السعة [lahā afwāh shadīdat al-saʿa] They have very wide mouths. That Posidonius held the same is clear, since to a dragon of a plethron's length [πλεθριαίῳ (plethriaiō)] in the Macra of Coele-Syria he attributes χάσμα ὥστ᾽ ἔφιππον δέξασθαι [chasma hōst' ephippon dexasthai], such a gape of the mouth that it could have taken in a rider together with his horse. So too Megasthenes, when he wrote that in India serpents (that is, dragons) grow to such a size that they swallow stags and bulls whole, on the authority of Pliny, book 8, chapter 14. [III, 234] Jeremiah agrees better with these, in whom the church would not say ^{a)}, Nebuchadnezzar has swallowed me up like a dragon, if the dragon were an animal of so small and harmless a gape.
The same prophet quite rightly compares with dragons the wild asses, which, exhausted for want of pasture,
— — — — look up to the sky, catching the breezes with open nostrils.

The wild asses (he says in chapter 14, verse 6) standing on the slopes draw in the wind like dragons. Yet we read that dragons draw to themselves by their breath not only the winds but also the birds flying over them. Mela, book 1, chapter 19: Around (the Rhyndacus) huge snakes are born, remarkable not only for their size but also because, when they have fled into its bed from the heat and the sun, they emerge and gape, and swallow the birds flying over them, however high and swiftly they are borne. Pliny writes the very same thing in book 8, chapter 14, as if from Metrodorus. And Aelian, book 2, chapter 21: Δράκοντες περὶ τῷ ποταμῷ τῷ καλουμένῳ Ῥυνδάκῳ, τὸ μέν τι τῆς σπείρας ἀπήρεισαν εἰς τὴν γῆν, τὸ δὲ λοιπὸν σῶμα ἀναστήσαντες πᾶν, ἀτρέμα, καὶ ἡσυχῆ τὴν φάρυγγα ἀνατείναντες, καὶ μέν τοι καὶ τὸ στόμα ἀνοίξαντες, εἶτα τὰ πτηνὰ ἕλκουσι, οἱονεὶ ἴϋγγι, τῷ ἄσθματι. τὰ δὲ εἰς ἐκείνων εἰσπίπτει γαστέρας, ὑπὸ τῆς περὶ αὐτῶν εἰσπνοῆς συρόμενα αὐτοῖς πτεροῖς. [Drakontes peri tō potamō tō kaloumenō Rhyndakō, to men ti tēs speiras apēreisan eis tēn gēn, to de loipon sōma anastēsantes pan, atrema, kai hēsychē tēn pharynga anateinantes, kai men toi kai to stoma anoixantes, eita ta ptēna helkousi, hoionei iyngi, tō asthmati. ta de eis ekeinōn eispiptei gasteras, hypo tēs peri autōn eispnoēs syromena autois pterois.] Around the river (of Pontus) named Rhyndacus, dragons, resting part of their coil on the ground, with the rest of the body raised, the neck stretched out silently and quietly, and the mouth gaping, draw the birds to themselves by their breath, as if by a love charm. And the birds fall into their belly, drawn wings and all by the dragons' breath. Philes, chapter 59, on dragons, [col. 437] reports the very same:

Δράκοντες Αἰθιόπων δέ τ᾽, εἰ θηρᾷν δεοῖ, Χαίνοντες ἀσθμαίνουσιν εἰς τὸν ἀέρα, Καὶ τῶν πετεινῶν τὰς κρεμαστὰς ἀγέλας, Ἴϋγξι θερμῆς εἰσπνοῆς καλουμένας, Καὶ σπωμένας ἄνωθεν εἰς γῆν ἀθρόας Ἐκ τῶν γνάθων ἕλκουσιν εἰς τὴν γαστέρα. [Drakontes Aithiopōn de t', ei thēran deoi, / Chainontes asthmainousin eis ton aera, / Kai tōn peteinōn tas kremastas agelas, / Iynxi thermēs eispnoēs kaloumenas, / Kai spōmenas anōthen eis gēn athroas / Ek tōn gnathōn helkousin eis tēn gastera.]

The Ethiopian dragons, when they need to hunt birds, gape and breathe out into the air; and the flocks of birds hovering aloft, beguiled by the charm of their warm breath and drawn down in numbers from on high to the earth, they draw from their jaws into their belly. Alluding to this, Tertullian, [III, 235] De corona militis, chapter 10, says: Even the earthly dragon absorbs birds from afar no less by its breath. Where Pamelius absurdly understands the basilisk by the name of dragon.

The most ancient of the Hebrews, who observed that dragons, as we have said, rear up and, gaping with wide-open jaws, breathe upwards, interpreted this as if, with mouth turned toward heaven, they were complaining to God about their lot with sighs and groans, and because, hateful to all and consigned to desert and deathly places, they dragged out with difficulty a life that was long indeed, but wretched. And accordingly Job, joining dragons with ostriches in chapter 30, verses 28 and 29, says: Rising up in the assembly I cried out. I was a brother of dragons, and a companion of ostriches. Micah likewise, chapter 1, verse 8: For this I will lament and howl, etc. I will make a lamentation like the dragons, and mourning like the ostriches. Perhaps they also have in view the dreadful hissings of dragons, with which the deserts resound. Aelian, book 15, chapter 21, on a certain dragon in India: Συριγμὸν μὲν οὖν ἀφῆκε μέγιστον, καὶ φύσημα, ὥστε ἐκπλῆξαι πάντας, καὶ ἐκταράξαι [Syrigmon men oun aphēke megiston, kai physēma, hōste ekplēxai pantas, kai ektaraxai]; It therefore emitted a very great hiss and blast, so that it terrified and confounded everyone (in Alexander's forces). And in book 16, chapter 39, the same author records another in Chios, δράκοντα μεγέθει μέγιστον, οὗπερ οὖν καὶ τὸν συριγμὸν ἐπιπεφρίκασιν οἱ τὴν Χίον κατοικοῦντες [drakonta megethei megiston, houper oun kai ton syrigmon epipephrikasin hoi tēn Chion katoikountes], a dragon of immense size, whose hiss all the inhabitants of Chios dreaded. Moreover, just as ostriches are called בנות יענה from their crying, so the name of dragons, תנים thannim, alludes to תנות thannoth, which the most ancient interpreters explain as θρηνεῖν [thrēnein], to lament, Iudic. XI, 40.

Many deny that the dragon has poison. Pliny, book 29, chapter 4: The dragon has no poisons. Aëtius: This animal does not cast poison. Isidore: It is harmless as regards poisons. Accordingly Nicander writes that those bitten by a dragon feel little pain. His words are:

— — — — οὐ μὲν ὅ γ᾽ αὐτῶς Ἐγχρίμψας ἤλγυνε, καὶ ἢν ἔκπαγλα χαλεφθῇ. Βληχρὸν γὰρ μυὸς οἷα νυχηβόρου ἐν χροῒ νύγμα Εἴδεται, αἱμαχθέντος ὑπὸ κραντῆρος ἀραιοῦ. [ou men ho g᾽ autōs Enchrimpsas ēlgyne, kai ēn ekpagla chalephthē. Blēchron gar myos hoia nychēborou en chroi nygma Eidetai, haimachthentos hypo krantēros araiou.]

It does not (like other serpents) cause equal pain when it strikes, even if it wounds severely. For from the weak, bloodied tooth a slight puncture appears on the skin, as from a mouse that devours by night (others read μυχηβόρου [mychēborou], that devours in the larder). Yet in his Song Moses says, Deut. XXXII, 33: The poison of dragons is their wine. And Sap. XVI, 10. Τοὺς δὲ υἱούς σου οὐδὲ ἰοβόλων δρακόντων ἐνίκησαν ὀδόντες [Tous de huious sou oude iobolōn drakontōn enikēsan odontes]; But your sons not even the teeth of poisonous dragons overcame. But, not to mention that the Hebrew תנין can be taken for [III, 236] any serpent, even if you understand it as dragon, it will be easy to reconcile these. For it is true that the dragons of Greece, of which Nicander and others speak, lack poison; except that they are read to eat noxious herbs on purpose, so as to make their bite more dangerous. Homer, Iliad χ´ [chi]:
Ὡς δὲ δράκων ἐπὶ χειῇ ὀρέστερος ἄνδρα μένῃσι Βεβρωκὼς κακὰ φάρμακα· — — [Hōs de drakōn epi cheiē oresteros andra menēsi Bebrōkōs kaka pharmaka]

As in its lair a mountain dragon, having fed on evil herbs, awaits a man. And Aelian, History book 6, chapter 4: Μέλλοντες δὲ τινα ἐλλοχᾷν, ἢ ἄνθρωπον, ἢ θῆρα, τὰς θανατηφόρους ῥίζας ἐσθίουσι [Mellontes de tina ellochan, ē anthrōpon, ē thēra, tas thanatēphorous rhizas esthiousi]; When they plot an ambush against a man or some wild beast, they eat deadly roots. In Eustathius others say ὅτι δράκων, ἐσθίων [col. 438] μύρμηκας, καὶ κανθαρίδας, ἰοῦ πληροῦται, καὶ εἰς λύσσαν ἄγεται [hoti drakōn, esthiōn myrmēkas, kai kantharidas, iou plēroutai, kai eis lyssan agetai], that the dragon, eating ants and cantharides, is filled with poison and driven to madness. Others likewise understand πόαν τινὰ χολῆς γεννητικὴν, ἣν ἐσθίων ὄφις εἰς χολὴν ἐρεθίζεται [poan tina cholēs gennētikēn, hēn esthiōn ophis eis cholēn erethizetai], a herb that generates bile, on eating which its bile is stirred up. But in Africa and Arabia there is no need of this device, since there it has a lethal poison. This was observed by Lucan in these words:
You too, dragons, who glide gleaming with golden splendour, harmless divinities in all lands, burning Africa makes pestilent. — —

Accordingly Heliodorus, treating of archers from the cinnamon-bearing region of Ethiopia: Οἱ δὲ μικροῖς μὲν τοῖς βέλεσιν, ἰῷ δὲ δρακόντων πεφραγμένοις ἐιστοξεύοντες, ὀξύν τινα καὶ ἀπότομον θάνατον ἐπέφερον [Hoi de mikrois men tois belesin, iō de drakontōn pephragmenois eistoxeuontes, oxyn tina kai apotomon thanaton epepheron]; But they, shooting arrows that were small indeed, but tainted with the poison of dragons, inflicted a swift and bitter death. And Prudentius, Hamartigenia, verse 481:
Behold! The Jebusite squadrons burn for battle: their golden darts, dipped in the blood of the dragon, flash with a deadly gleam. — — —
And Apollinaris, Psalm 73:
Ὤλεσας ἰοβόλων κεφαλὰς ῥοθίοισι δρακόντων, [Ōlesas iobolōn kephalas rhothioisi drakontōn,]
In the waves you destroyed the heads of the dragons that spew poison. And Psalm 90:
Ἰοβόλον δὲ δράκοντα ποσὶν καὶ θῆρα πατήσεις, [Iobolon de drakonta posin kai thēra patēseis,]

You shall trample the poisonous dragon and the lion under your feet. And Leo Africanus, book 9: [III, 237] The dragons of Atlas are extremely poisonous: and if by chance they either touch or bite anyone, they soften and weaken the flesh. Indeed in Africa and Numidia all serpents have a more deadly poison than in other lands. Hence Horace, book 3, Ode 10,
Nor gentler in spirit than Moorish snakes.
And at the end of book 2 of the Satires,
— — — — as if Canidia had breathed on them, worse than African serpents.

Everyone knows that serpents are extremely fond of wine. For the Philosopher teaches this in History, book 8, chapter 4: Οἱ δὲ ὄφεις καὶ πρὸς τὸν οἶνόν εἰσιν ἀκρατοὺς. Διὸ θηρεύουσί τινες καὶ τοὺς ἔχεις εἰς ὀστράκια, διὰ τὸ τιθέναι οἶνον εἰς τὰς αἱμασίας· λαμβάνονται γὰρ μεθύοντες. [Hoi de opheis kai pros ton oinon eisin akratous. Dio thēreuousi tines kai tous echeis eis ostrakia, dia to tithenai oinon eis tas haimasias; lambanontai gar methyontes.] Serpents are greedy for wine. Accordingly some hunt vipers by setting out wine in earthenware vessels by the hedges: for they are caught drunk. And Pliny, book 10, chapter 72: Serpents, when there is opportunity, especially crave wine. But that by drinking wine the poison of serpents and dragons becomes sharper and stronger I have learned from no other source than the Chaldee Jonathan, who, for the words of Moses, The poison of dragons is their poison, Deut. XXXII, 33, has this in his Paraphrase: הי כמרירתהון דתניניא כי הנך הוון מן חמרהון בגין כן יהי מריר כס דלוות דישתון ביום פורענותהון, Behold! as is the gall of dragons when they are from their wine (that is, after they have drunk wine), so shall be the gall of the cup from which they shall drink on the day of their punishment.

The dragon seeks out solitary places, τὴν ἐρημίαν πρὸ τῶν ἀστικῶν διατριβῶν [tēn erēmian pro tōn astikōn diatribōn], says Aelian, book 6, chapter 63. Plutarch therefore acutely denies, in his book On the Obsolescence of Oracles, that what they say is true, that Delphi was once deserted because a dragon lived there; rather, the dragon lived there because the place was deserted. Ἡ γὰρ ἐρημία τὸ θηρίον ἐπηγάγετο, μᾶλλον ἢ τὸ θηρίον ἐποίησε τὴν ἐρημίαν. [Hē gar erēmia to thērion epēgageto, mallon ē to thērion epoiēse tēn erēmian.] This is why the Prophets so often ^{b)} foretell that the most populous cities will become the dwellings of dragons, or will be inhabited by dragons. By these words they threaten them with utter desolation. So Aquila rendered not badly at Ps. XLIV, 20: You have crushed us ἐν τόπῳ ἀοικήτῳ [en topō aoikētō], in an uninhabitable place, for what is in Hebrew in the place of dragons. But although dragons often live in thirsty places, yet, where they are free to choose, they settle much more gladly in well-watered valleys. Thus also of real dragons, in its own [col. 439] [III, 238] way, what Isaiah ^{c)} prophesied of mystical dragons, that is, of the nations far from the knowledge of the true God but to be called in due time, is true: that the dragons will glorify God, when he has put waters in the desert and rivers in the wilderness. And in Nehem. II, 13. the dragon's spring near Jerusalem seems to be named from a dragon that used to lurk there while the city lay desolate. So Pausanias in his Boeotica describes a spring near the river Ismenus, over which a dragon was set as guardian, by Mars, of course. And Philostratus, book 3, chapter 2, observes that Homer placed the dragon at Aulis by a spring, περὶ κρήνην [peri krēnēn]. This is far more probable than what Villalpandus conjectures, that this little spring nourished those large fish which in Hebrew are called תנים. But it also seems forced, what a learned man asserts, that the spring of Siloam is named from its slow and creeping flow, of which Es. VIII, 6. The Greeks render πηγὴν τῶν συκῶν [pēgēn tōn sykōn], the spring of the figs, because for תנים they read תאנים. The Syriac, however, has ܥܝܢܐ ܕܬܠܠܐ, the spring of the hills, as if it had read תלים.

In Apocal. XII, 9. the devil is called the great dragon and the ancient serpent, which come to almost the same thing. For it is reported that serpents, over a long course of years, at length become dragons. Moreover, not just any demon is called dragon, but the one who seduced Eve. Most hold, further, that he is the prince of demons, and that the name dragon signifies that he is as eminent among the demons as a great dragon is among the common run of serpents. Accordingly Philo Judaeus ^{d)}, who wrote before John, also calls this very demon a dragon. Ταῦτα δὲ, he says, οὕτω μὲν λεγόμενα φάσμασιν ἔοικε, καὶ τέρασι, δράκων ἀνθρώπου προϊέμενος φωνὴν, καὶ ἐνσοφιστεύων ἀκακωτάτοις ἤθεσι, καὶ πιθανότησιν εὐπαραγώγοις γυναῖκα ἀπατῶν· [Tauta de ... houtō men legomena phasmasin eoike, kai terasi, drakōn anthrōpou proiemenos phōnēn, kai ensophisteuōn akakōtatois ēthesi, kai pithanotēsin euparagōgois gynaika apatōn;] These things, as they are related, might seem closer to apparitions and portents: a dragon uttering human [col. 440] words, and corrupting the most innocent character with subtleties, and deceiving the woman with persuasions by which she is easily imposed upon. The Hebrews too call him הנחש הקדמוני, the ancient serpent. This was observed long ago by Drusius on this passage, and by Paulus Fagius on Genesis. Nor is the reason for the name obscure. First, he seduced Eve in the form of a serpent. Second, Satan attacks us secretly and from ambush, and
— — — a snake lurks in the grass.

Third, as the serpent is crafty, Gen. III, 1., so the devil is by far the most cunning. Hence he is said to have seduced Eve ἐν τῇ πανουργίᾳ αὐτοῦ [en tē panourgia autou], 2 Cor. XI, 3. Fourth, as the poison of the serpent is spread through the whole body, so the poison of the demon is spread through the whole soul. Finally, nothing is more hateful to man than the serpent, nothing that we flee more.

[III, 239] Hence Theophrastus in the Characters, on cavilling: Τὰ δὴ τῶν ἠθῶν μὴ ἁπλᾶ, ἀλλ᾽ ἐπίβουλα, φυλάττεσθαι μᾶλλον δεῖ, ἢ τοὺς ἔχεις [Ta dē tōn ēthōn mē hapla, all᾽ epiboula, phylattesthai mallon dei, ē tous echeis]; Characters that are not simple but treacherous must be shunned more than vipers. And in Theocritus, Praxinoë, to show that she dreads above all horses that throw their riders, says:
Ἵππον, καὶ τὸν ψυχρὸν ὄφιν, τὰ μάλιστα δεδοίκω· [Hippon, kai ton psychron ophin, ta malista dedoikō;]
A horse and the cold snake I fear most. And Plautus in the Mercator:
Your wife, of course, is in the country, whom a while ago you said you hated as much as snakes. — —
As Horace in the first book of the Epistles:
— — he will shun it worse than a dog and a snake. — — —
So between the race of demons and that of men there is a bitter hatred, of which Gen. III, 15. speaks. But we touch on this only in passing, since these matters belong to another place.
[III, 240] APPENDIX TO THE THIRD BOOK.
On Serpents in General.

[So that nothing that could be in any way useful and profitable should be missing from our edition of Bochart's work, it seemed good to append to this book, by way of a supplement, what Bochart discussed in vol. I, book I, Chapter IV on serpents in general, since it contains much that does not recur in the rest of the work, yet deserves not to be neglected by the interpreter of the O. T., especially of Chapter III of Genesis.]

The serpent is ζῶον ἑρπετὸν, ἔναιμον, φολιδωτὸν [zōon herpeton, enaimon, pholidōton], a creeping animal, endowed with blood, covered with scales. Its proper part is the גחון gachon, Gen. III, 14., that is, the elongated belly on which it creeps. The Philosopher ^{a)}: Τὴν δὲ κοιλίαν ὁ ὄφις ἔχει, οἷον ἔντερον εὐρυχωρέστερον [Tēn de koilian ho ophis echei, hoion enteron eurychōresteron]. There are those who think that the serpent at its creation was four-footed, or at least two-footed like dragons, and that its now creeping on its belly belongs to the punishment. But it does not seem likely to me that God changed anything in the nature of the serpent on account of man's sin. Only what belonged to its nature was turned into a punishment, as nakedness in man and childbirth in woman. Nor indeed is it sufficiently certain that any dragon is two-footed, or, as Pliny says ^{b)}, that serpents have been seen with goose's feet. Augustine, book 3 De Gen. ad lit., expressly asserts that dragons are without feet. And the Philosopher, in the book On the Progression of Animals, proves at length that neither two nor four feet could suffice a serpent because of the enormous length of its body, and that it could not have more, because τῶν ἐναίμων μηδὲν οἷον τ᾽ εἶναι πλείοσι σημείοις κινεῖσθαι, ἢ τέτταρσιν [tōn enaimōn mēden hoion t᾽ einai pleiosi sēmeiois kineisthai, ē tettarsin]. Hence he concludes that τὴν ἀποδίαν [tēn apodian] is necessary in the serpent.

In the curse of the serpent it is rightly said of the seed of the woman, It shall bruise your head, Gen. III, 15., because in the serpent the head is by far the most important part, and while it is unharmed the serpent rarely succumbs. Isidore, Orig. book 12, ch. 4: Pliny says, if it is to be believed, that the head of a serpent, even if it has escaped with only two fingers' length of body, nevertheless lives. For, as Aelian testifies ^{c)}, τὴν καρδίαν κεκλήρωται ἐπὶ τῇ φάρυγγι [tēn kardian keklērōtai epi tē pharyngi], it has its heart allotted in [III, 241] the throat, near the head, whereas in other animals the heart occupies the middle of the chest. Hence it is that Epaminondas, in order to drive the Thebans straight against the line of the Lacedaemonians, ^{d)} Μέγιστον ἔχιν συλλαβὼν ἔδειξεν αὐτοῖς, καὶ πάντων ἐναντίον τὴν κεφαλὴν τοῦ θηρίου συντρίψας, Ὁρᾶτε, ἔφη, ὅτι τὸ λοιπὸν σῶμα ἄχρηστον, τῆς κεφαλῆς οἰχομένης. οὕτω δὴ ἢν τὰς τῶν πολεμίων κεφαλὰς, τὸ Λακωνικὸν τοῦτο συντρίψωμεν, τὸ λοιπὸν σῶμα τῶν συμμάχων ἄχρηστον. [Megiston echin syllabōn edeixen autois, kai pantōn enantion tēn kephalēn tou thēriou syntripsas, Horate, ephē, hoti to loipon sōma achrēston, tēs kephalēs oichomenēs. houtō dē ēn tas tōn polemiōn kephalas, to Lakōnikon touto syntripsōmen, to loipon sōma tōn symmachōn achrēston.] seized a very large serpent and showed it to them, and having crushed its head in the sight of all, said: You see that, once the head is taken away, the rest of the body is useless. So, if we crush the heads of the enemy, namely this Laconian one, the rest of the body of the allies will be of no use. For this reason the serpent in a fight is almost wholly intent on keeping its head out of danger. Epiphanius in the Physiologus, ch. 15: Ὅλον τὸ σῶμα παραδίδωσι, τὴν κεφαλὴν μόνην φυλάσσει [Holon to sōma paradidōsi, tēn kephalēn monēn phylassei]. And against the Ophites, Heresy 37: Ἐν τῷ διώκεσθαι, γινώσκων ὅτι ἐν τῇ κεφαλῇ αὐτοῦ ἡ πᾶσα ζωὴ αὐτοῦ τυγχάνει, ὅλον τὸ σῶμα ἐνειλήσας ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτοῦ κρύπτει μὲν τὸ κρανίον ἑαυτοῦ, παραδίδωσι δὲ τὸ ἄλλο σῶμα· [En tō diōkesthai, ginōskōn hoti en tē kephalē autou hē pasa zōē autou tynchanei, holon to sōma eneilēsas epi tēn kephalēn autou kryptei men to kranion heautou, paradidōsi de to allo sōma] When attacked by someone, since it perceives that its whole life resides in its head, it coils its whole body around its head and hides its skull, but gives up the rest of its body. Chrysostom on Psal. CXIV.: Ὁ ὄφις τὸ λοιπὸν σῶμα προΐεται, ὥστε τὴν κεφαλὴν διασῶσαι [Ho ophis to loipon sōma proietai, hōste tēn kephalēn diasōsai]. The serpent exposes the rest of its body in order to preserve its head. Caesarius, Dialogue 4, Question 192: Ὁ γὰρ ὄφις ὑπὸ βροτοῦ δυνάμει καταλεφθεὶς, ὅλον μὲν τῷ παίοντι τὸ σῶμα περοΐεται, τὴν δὲ κεφαλὴν ἄτρωτον φρουρεῖν μηχανᾶται [Ho gar ophis hypo brotou dynamei katalephtheis, holon men tō paionti to sōma peroietai, tēn de kephalēn atrōton phrourein mēchanatai]. For the serpent, when seized by force by a man, offers its whole body to the one striking it, but tries to keep its head unharmed. Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, Epist. 126: Ὅσαις γὰρ ἂν περιστάσεσι καὶ πληγαῖς ὁ ὄφις συνέχηται, τὴν ἑαυτοῦ φυλάττει κεφαλὴν ἀβλαβῆ· [Hosais gar an peristasesi kai plēgais ho ophis synechētai, tēn heautou phylattei kephalēn ablabē] For whatever mishaps and blows the serpent is beset by, it keeps its head unharmed. And the other Isidore, namely of Seville, Orig. book 12, ch. 4: It offers its whole body in place of its head to those striking it. Tzetzes, Chil. 9, ch. 263:
τυπτόμενος εἰς φόνον, Παντοιοτρόπως τὴν κεφαλὴν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ συγκρύπτει. [typtomenos eis phonon, Pantoiotropōs tēn kephalēn tēn heautou synkryptei.]

Does what the Son of Sirach writes ^{e)} belong here: Οὐκ ἔστι κεφαλὴ ὑπὲρ κεφαλὴν ὄφεως [Ouk esti kephalē hyper kephalēn opheōs]; There is no head above the head of a serpent? I do not think so, because then the sense would be rather obscure. Without doubt, therefore, the author of the book had written in Hebrew לא ראש על ראש הנחש, which should be translated, There is no poison above the poison of the serpent. For ראש means poison as well as head. Thus Deut. XXXII, 33. Their wine, ראש פתנים, the poison of asps. Whoever rendered it the head of asps would be utterly wide of the mark. [III, 242] That poison is partly in the gall, Iob. XX, 14. The gall of asps within him. Pliny, book 11, ch. 37: Let no one be surprised that the gall is the poison of serpents. And book 29, ch. 6: The most careful authors write that this is nothing other than the gall of serpents, and that it reaches them from there through the veins under the spine. Partly also in the teeth, Eccles. XXXIX, 35., and in a certain small bladder under the tongue; therefore Iob. XX, 16. The tongue of the viper shall slay him.

The tips of the tongue are λεπτὰ ὥσπερ τρίχες [lepta hōsper triches] ^{f)}, as thin as hairs. With an eye to this David says, Psal. CXL, 3. They have sharpened their tongues like serpents. Plautus more than once calls them bilingues [two-tongued]. Thus in the Persa: Like a creeping beast, he is two-tongued and wicked. And in the Asinaria Libanus invites Philenium to a kiss thus: Be a creeping beast, so that I may have a double tongue. That is, if we believe Salmasius, serpents flicker their tongue with so tremulous a motion that it seems not single but double. In the same way those who brandished and shook a sarissa were said sarissam duplicare [to double the sarissa], as though by shaking it they made it double. Hence Hesychius: Πτύσσει· κραδαίνει, τὰ δόρατα διπλοῖ [Ptyssei; kradainei, ta dorata diploi], that is, he brandishes the spears and doubles them. And in the Apology of Apuleius, Laelius calls ἴϋγγας [iyngas] inlices bicodulas [two-tailed lures], because by the constant vibration of the tail they make it in some measure double, and so seem to have two tails. From this motion of the tail the Iynx is called σεισοπυγὶς [seisopygis], and motacilla [wagtail]. That some of the ancients held this very opinion is shown by these words of Isidore on the serpent, Orig. book 12, ch. 4: No animal moves its tongue with such speed, so much so that it seems to have a triple tongue, though it has only one. But these things, however plausible, are by no means true. For the serpent is not called bilinguis by Plautus because of the swift vibration of its tongue, but because it has a forked one, as he himself testifies in the Poenulus: With forked tongue, like a creeping beast. Accordingly the Philosopher asserts, in the place cited above, δικρόαν αὐτῶν εἶναι τὴν γλῶτταν ἄκραν [dikroan autōn einai tēn glōttan akran], that the tip of their tongue is cleft. Hence the Arabs in Damir, in the chapter الحية [al-ḥayya], or On the serpent: لسانها مشقوق ولذلك يظن بعض الناس ان لها لسانين [lisānuhā mashqūq wa-li-dhālika yaẓunnu baʿḍ al-nās anna lahā lisānayn] Its tongue is divided; for this reason some think it has two tongues. And in the chapter الضب [al-ḍabb], or On the land crocodile: ولما سال الامام ابو حنيفة عن ذكر الضب فقال انه كلسان الحية اصل واحد له فرعان [wa-lammā saʾala al-imām Abū Ḥanīfa ʿan dhakar al-ḍabb fa-qāla innahu ka-lisān al-ḥayya aṣl wāḥid lahu farʿān] And when the priest Abuchanipha had inquired about the penis of the land crocodile, he said that it is like the tongue of the serpent, which has one root but is forked. Others assert that it is three-forked. Thus Pliny ^{g)}: The tongue of serpents is very thin, and three-forked. The poets generally follow this. Virgil, Georg. book 3 and Aen. book 2:
[III, 243] Towering toward the Sun, it flickers in its mouth with three-forked tongues.
Ovid, on the dragon slain by Cadmus, Metam. book 3:
— — — its whole body swells with poison, and three tongues flicker.
And on the dragon in Colchis, guardian of the golden fleece, Metam. book 7:
Who, conspicuous for his crest and his three tongues.
Seneca in the Medea, line 686:
Here the savage serpent drags its immense body, and thrusts out its three-cleft tongue.
Silius book 6, line 222:
— — — the tongue, brandished through the air with three-cleft motion, flickers, and leaping up licks the sky.
And line 264:
— — and now, now with the tip of its three-forked tongue it was licking the back of the steed wearied by the struggle.
Statius on the Python, book 1 of the Thebaid, line 565:
— — while, stretched out, it gapes with three-forked mouth at the Castalian springs.
And on the serpent by which Archemorus was slain, book 5, line 580:
— the spear flies quivering, and enters the gaping jaws of the monster, and cuts the fierce bonds of the three-forked tongue.

Should we refer to this the fact that the slanderer, who thrusts out his tongue against anyone and flickers it in the manner of a serpent, is assigned a triple tongue in the Chaldee paraphrase, Iob. XXXVI, 33. Ps. CI, 5. and CXL, 12. Eccles. X, 11. etc.? It certainly seems so. Nor do I interpret otherwise these words of Sirach XXVIII, 15. Γλῶσσα τρίτη πολλοὺς ἐσάλευσεν [Glōssa tritē pollous esaleusen], and verse 17, Γλῶσσα τρίτη γυναῖκας ἀνδρείας ἐξέβαλε [Glōssa tritē gynaikas andreias exebale]. Others explain them differently, as we shall observe below.
But this interpretation is strongly confirmed by the words of the Psalmist, in which the slanderer's tongue is compared with the tongue of a serpent.

I add, on the authority of the Arabs, a fact passed over by the Roman and Greek writers: that some serpents have a tongue that is not only sharp but armed with a sting, or else [III, 244] a sting in the snout and nose; that others, like scorpions, also strike with the tail; and that others prick with a double sting, one at each end. Alcamus: النكّاز حية لا ينكز الا بانفه ليس له فم لا يعرف ذنبه من راسه لدقته من اخبث الحيات [al-nakkāz ḥayya lā yankuzu illā bi-anfihi laysa lahu fam lā yuʿrafu dhanabuhu min raʾsihi li-diqqatihi min akhbath al-ḥayyāt] Nicchaz, a serpent that pricks only with its nose, as if it had no mouth, whose head is so slender that it cannot be distinguished from its tail. It is the worst kind of serpent. For نكز [nakaza] nahaza, said of a serpent, means to prick with the nose or with the snout. In the same place: ذو الطرفين من الحيات لها ابرتان احدهما في انفها والاخري في ذنبها [dhū al-ṭarafayn min al-ḥayyāt lahā ibratān iḥdāhumā fī anfihā wa-al-ukhrā fī dhanabihā] Dultaraphina, a kind of serpent with a double sting, one of which is in the nose, the other in the tail. Hence Solomon distinguishes the prick of a serpent from its bite, Prov. XXIII, 32: You will bite like a serpent, and like a basilisk יפרש you will prick. So in Yucatán, bordering on New Spain, a serpent called Polpoch, because its hiss seems to give roughly this sound, is written both to bite with its mouth and to prick with a sting in its tail ^{h)}). And in South America, among the Chiribichenses, Peter Martyr ^{i)}) mentions asps that strike with the tail like scorpions.

The hiss of serpents is terrible, Sap. XVII, 9. yet thin, as the Philosopher observes ^{k)}? Therefore Jeremiah, ch. 46, verse 22, speaking of Egypt, which was to be crushed by the Chaldeans, says: Her voice shall go like a serpent's; because, weighed down by servitude, she will scarcely dare to open her mouth and mutter. Like this is Esa. XXIX, 4. You shall be brought low, you shall speak from the ground, and your speech shall be low out of the dust. But the Syriac translator renders the passage of Jeremiah thus: ܩܠܗ ܕܚܝܠܐ ܐܝܟ ܚܘܝܐ ܕܪܚܫ The voice of the army shall be like that of a creeping serpent. And the Chaldee: קל כחוש זיניהון כחון זחלין, The crash of the clashing of their arms shall be like that of creeping serpents. As if he compared the crash of arms in the forces of the Chaldeans with the rustling that the skins of certain serpents make as they creep, for instance the cerastes or the haemorrhous, of which Nicander says in the Theriaca,

— — — φολίσιν δὲ, καὶ οἴμῳ Παῦρον ὑποψοφέων καλάμης χύσιν οἷα διέρπει· [pholisin de, kai oimō Pauron hypopsopheōn kalamēs chysin hoia dierpei] — — — as it creeps it gives a faint murmur from the rubbing of its scales, like trodden reeds.

And Aelian, On Animals book 15, ch. 13: Ἕρπει δὲ ἥσυχος ἐπιθλίβων τὰς τῆς νηδύος φολίδας, λοξὸν δὲ οἶμον πρόεισιν· ἠρέμα γοῦν ὑπηχεῖ. [Herpei de hēsychos epithlibōn tas tēs nēdyos pholidas, loxon de oimon proeisin; ērema goun hypēchei.] It creeps slowly [III, 245] pressing the scales of its belly, and advances by a winding path, and makes a gentle rustling. And of the cerastes Aetius ^{l)}: In creeping it makes a sound like a hiss. Avicenna ^{m)} too, just like Nicander, writes that when the cerastes and the haemorrhous creep, a sound of slight rustling is made, like قصبا الغاب خشخشة [qaṣabā al-ghāb khashkhasha], the crackling of reeds. Now hear the trifles of the Rabbis. Eliezer in the Chapters, and R. Selomo on Jeremiah, think he is speaking of that ancient serpent which, when it was deprived of its feet as punishment for sin, cried out so horribly that it was heard from one end of the world to the other. So Jonathan, Exod. VII, 9. says that all the ends of the earth heard the cry of the serpent when it was stripped, from the foundation of the world.

Serpents live either in waters, Amos IX, 3. or in dry places, Deut. VIII, 15. for instance on rocks, Prov. XXX, 19. in hedges, Eccles. X, 8. in holes in the ground, Es. XI, 8. Nicander embraces these three in one verse, speaking of deer which, to track down a serpent,
Τρόχμαλα θ᾽ αἱμασίας τε καὶ εἰλύους ἐρέουσι, [Trochmala th᾽ haimasias te kai eilyous ereousi] Seek out rocks, and hedges, and the hiding places of caves.

Serpents are reckoned among the παμφάγοις [pamphagois]; for they eat both flesh and herbs, and are λιχνότατοι τῶν ζώων [lichnotatoi tōn zōōn] ^{n)}, more given to dainties than other animals. So dust is assigned to the serpent as food, Gen. III, 14. Esa. LXV, 25. and Mich. VII, 17. not because it feeds on dust alone, but because, crawling on the ground, it cannot help taking dust into its mouth together with other food. Thus David in mourning complains that he has eaten ashes like bread, Ps. CII, 10. because, lying prostrate in ashes, he ate bread thrown on the ground. The Talmudists, however, in the tractate On the Sabbath: טועמין את הארץ כחויא, They ate earth like a serpent. And Nicander, of the chersydrus ^{o)}, when the water has dried up completely and failed it, νέμεται διψήρεας ὄγμους [nemetai dipsēreas ogmous], feeds on the dry furrows. And Philes, ch. 59, of a certain serpent of India, which seems to be a species of seps,
Νωδὸς γάρ ἐστι, καὶ ψιλὸν χοῦν ἐσθίει. [Nōdos gar esti, kai psilon choun esthiei.] It lives on dust alone, and is toothless.
But other animals too are thought to feed on the same food. Among them are earthworms and worms. Plautus in the Casina, Act 1.

But afterwards, unless you eat vetch in the country, or earth, like an earthworm. [III, 246] And الحباحب [al-ḥabāḥib], the glow-worm, of which Algiahid says: غذاوها التراب لم تشبع منه قط خوق ان يغني تراب الارض فتهلك جوعا [ghidhāwuhā al-turāb lam tashbaʿ minhu qaṭṭ khawq an yughnī turāb al-arḍ fa-tahlik jūʿan] "Its food is dust, with which it is never sated, only because it fears that the dust of the earth may run out and it may thus perish of hunger." So among the water birds the مالك الحزين [mālik al-ḥazīn] malich alhazin, called by others البلشون [al-balshūn] balscun, that is, the ardea [heron], which the Arabs write uses water so sparingly, and abstains from drinking so long, that it dies of thirst, lest the water run out if it drank a little more freely. This is a symbol of the avaricious rich man who, for fear of want, cheats his own appetite. Scorpions too are said to take earth as food. Bardesanes in Eusebius, De Praepar. book 6: Σκόρπιος γῆν ἐσθίει [Skorpios gēn esthiei]. Pliny, book 10, ch. 72: "Scorpions live on earth." And the mole, in the Porta coeli, fol. 22. ch.: ומן היסוד העפרי יתהוה באשות הנקרא טלפא אשר מזונה העפר, "And from the element of earth the mole was made, whose food is dust." As Vincent ^{p)} says of the same animal: "It lives in the earth, it lives on worms as food, and in hunger it also eats earth." Indeed Cardano ^{q)} says he has seen birds feeding on earth. But he doubts whether this happened under the compulsion of hunger, or so that they might extract something suited to their nature, whether saltiness or something else. Thus, according to the Philosopher ^{r)}, Τοὺς λύκους φασὶν, ὅταν πεινῶσιν, ἐσθίειν τινὰ γῆν [Tous lykous phasin, hotan peinōsin, esthiein tina gēn]. "Wolves, when hungry, are said to eat a certain kind of earth." And in Pisides, in the Hexaëmeron:
Λύκοι δὲ τὴν γῆν, οἱ λαγοὶ δὲ κανθάρους. [Lykoi de tēn gēn, hoi lagoi de kantharous.] "And wolves eat earth, and hares beetles":
but only in sickness, as medicine. But Vincent ^{s)} reports that elephants die if they eat earth, yet that some become so accustomed to this food that the habit of it is to them a second nature.

Aristotle ^{t)} and Pliny ^{u)} write that serpents are ὠοτοκεῖν [ōotokein], lay eggs outside the body, and εἰς τὴν γῆν ἐπωάζειν [eis tēn gēn epōazein], incubate them in the earth, and that these hatch in the following year. So also Esaias XXXIV, 15: "There the קפוז, the acontias, shall make its nest, and lay, and hatch eggs, which it will brood under its shadow": and LIX, 5: "They have hatched the eggs of the basilisk."

In Genes. III, 1, the serpent is read to have been ערום above every beast of the earth. Others rightly render ערום as πανοῦργον [panourgon], cunning, crafty, astute, wily, shifty; the LXX alone render it φρόνιμον [phronimon], prudent. Yet I would by no means wish to bring a charge against them on this account, since elsewhere too ערום means prudent, as frequently in Proverbs ^{x)}. And Christ himself seems to confirm this interpretation, [III, 247] when he exhorts the disciples to be prudent as serpents, Matth. X, 16., using, if I am not mistaken, the same word as Moses. Although these words of the Apostle, 2 Cor. XI, 3., allude to the other meaning: Ὁ ὄφις Εὔαν ἐξεπάτησεν ἐν τῇ πανουργίᾳ αὐτοῦ [Ho ophis Euan exepatēsen en tē panourgia autou], "The serpent beguiled Eve by his cunning." In what sense either πανουργία [panourgia] or φρόνησις [phronēsis] is attributed to brute animals I shall say elsewhere. Here I shall only observe that this phrase is wrongly confirmed from Theophrastus, whose book Περὶ τῶν ζώων, ὅσα λέγεται φρονεῖν [Peri tōn zōōn, hosa legetai phronein] is cited by Laertius ^{y)}. For there φθονεῖν [phthonein] must be read instead of φρονεῖν [phronein], as we know from Photius, who gives us a summary of this book in Author 178.

To the cunning of the serpent I refer the fact that the cerastes, or ammodytes, standing in the way and hiding in the sands, whose colour it shares, bites the hoofs of the horse, Genes. XLIX, 17., and lies in wait for the heel of man, Gen. III, 15., and, putting out only its little horns, which resemble grains of corn, catches small birds flying up as if to food. Likewise the fact that, according to Lucian ^{z)}, dipsades lie in ambush by the ostrich eggs, which the Garamantes greatly covet, ready to bite those who approach. Accordingly the Philosopher ^{a)} reports that serpents are μάλιστα ἐπιβούλους [malista epiboulous], most treacherous. And in Aesop the crab, having made a partnership with the serpent, urged it μεταβαλέσθαι τῆς πανουργίας [metabalesthai tēs panourgias], to change its cunning: ὁ δὲ οὐδοτιοῦν ἑαυτὸν παρεῖχε πειθόμενον [ho de oudotioun heauton pareiche peithomenon], but it showed itself not at all compliant.

The Physiologus of Epiphanius offers four proofs of the serpent's prudence. First, when it senses old age coming on, it seeks a rock and ῥαγαδαστεύει [ragadasteuei], προκύψας δὲ διὰ τῆς ὀπῆς ὠθεῖται περάσαι, καὶ ἐκβάλλει τὸ γῆρας [prokypsas de dia tēs opēs ōtheitai perasai, kai ekballei to gēras], it slips into a crevice, and, bending forward, strives to pass through the hole, and puts off its old age. And this all assert with one voice. Second, although it flees from a clothed man, when it sees the same man naked, καταθαῤῥεῖ αὐτοῦ [katatharrei autou], it attacks him confidently. This too might seem consistent with reason; yet others expressly teach the opposite. Eustathius in the Hexaemeron: Ἐὰν δὲ γυμνὸν θεάσηται ἄνθρωπον οὐ πρόσεισιν· εἰ δὲ ἐνδεδυμένον, ἐφάλλεται [Ean de gymnon theasētai anthrōpon ou proseisin; ei de endedymenon, ephalletai]; If it has seen a naked man, it does not approach; but if it has seen a clothed one, it attacks. Jerome, or whoever is the author of the Letter to Praesidius under Jerome's name: The snake fears a naked man, and pursues a clothed one. Isidore, book 12, ch. 4: It is said, moreover, that the serpent does not dare to touch a naked man. Damir: ومن عجيب امره انها تهرب من الرجل العريان [wa-min ʿajīb amrihi annahā tahrub min al-rajul al-ʿuryān] Among the marvels of its nature is that it flees from a naked man. And Olaus writes that he has experienced this not rarely. Isidore, he says, offers a favourable word about the nature of serpents, that they never harm a naked and sleeping man [III, 248]: and this happened to me in boyhood and youth, when I very often encountered serpents without harm. The same author offers a third proof of the serpent's prudence: that when attacked by a man it keeps only its head unharmed and exposes the rest of its body. Since I have already said much about this, I shall add only this from Caesarius, Dial. 4, Quaest. 190: Κατευναζόμενος δὲ, καὶ καθεύδων (ὁ ὄφις) τροχίζων ἑαυτὸν, μέσην ὅλου τοῦ σώματος κεφαλὴν ἀσφαλίζεται, οἱονεὶ τειχίῳ τῷ ἐφεπομένῳ ὁλκῷ περιοχυρῶν αὐτήν [Kateunazomenos de, kai katheudōn (ho ophis) trochizōn heauton, mesēn holou tou sōmatos kephalēn asphalizetai, hoionei teichiō tō epheponemō holkō periochyrōn autēn]; When the serpent gives itself to rest in order to sleep, coiling itself up, it secures its head in the middle of its whole body, encircling it with the following length of its body as with a wall. Fourth, when it comes to a spring to drink, οὐ φέρει τὸν ἰὸν, ἀλλά γε ἀφεὶς αὐτὸν ἐν τῇ νεοττίᾳ, οὕτω καθαρὸς πορεύεται [ou pherei ton ion, alla ge apheis auton en tē neottia, houtō katharos poreuetai], it does not carry its poison along, but leaving it in its nest, it approaches thus pure. The same author sets this out as follows in Haer. 37: Οὐ συμπαραλαμβάνει τὸν ἰὸν μεθ᾽ ἑαυτοῦ, ἀλλὰ ἐν τῷ φωλεῷ καταλιμπάνει, καὶ οὕτως ἐλθὼν λαμβάνει τὸ πόμα τῶν ὑδάτων [Ou symparalambanei ton ion meth' heautou, alla en tō phōleō katalimpanei, kai houtōs elthōn lambanei to poma tōn hydatōn]; It does not bring its poison out with it, but leaves it in its lair, and approaching thus takes its drink of the waters. And Eustathius in the Hexaemeron: Ὅταν δὲ διψήσῃ τὸν ἰὸν πρότερον ἀποτίθεται, καὶ οὕτως ἐκπίνει τὸ ὕδωρ ἐκ τῆς πηγῆς [Hotan de dipsēsē ton ion proteron apotithetai, kai houtōs ekpinei to hydōr ek tēs pēgēs]; When it is thirsty, it first lays down its poison, and so drinks water from the spring: namely, lest the poison, congealed by the water, should kill it, as the author of the Letter to Praesidius adds. Not unlike this is what many write, that the viper, when about to mate with the moray, first vomits out its poison, as if αἰδουμένην τὸν γάμον [aidoumenēn ton gamon], revering the marriage, as Basil says, Hom. 7 on the Hexaem. But Andreas ^{b)} rejects this as fabulous in his book Περὶ τῶν ψευδῶς πεπιστευμένων [Peri tōn pseudōs pepisteumenōn]. Although, besides Basil ^{c)} and Ambrose, it has as authorities Nicander ^{d)}, Aelian ^{e)}, Oppian ^{f)}, Licinius Macer ^{g)}, Achilles Tatius ^{h)}, Philes in the Iambics ^{i)}, and Isidore ^{k)}, and others in no small number.

To these may be added from Pliny that the serpent, when its sight has been dimmed in its winter hiding place, anoints and refreshes its eyes with fennel; and if its scales have grown stiff, it scrapes itself on the thorns of the juniper; and that the dragon relieves its spring nausea with the juice of lettuce. It is more probable that these things happen by natural skill than by some θεηλάτῳ [theēlatō] impulse, as the Arabs imagine. Among them is الزمخشري [al-Zamakhsharī] Azzammachsari, a writer fabulous above others, whose words are: حكي ان الافعي اذا اتت عليها الف سنة عميت وقد الهمها الله ان تمسح عينيها بورق الرازيانج الرطب فير اليها بصرها وربما كان [III, 249] في برية بينها وبين الريف مسيرة ثلثة ايام فتطوي تلك المسافة علي طولها وعلي عماها حتي تهاجم في بعض البساتين علي شجر الرازيانج لاتحظيه فتحك به عينها فترجع باصرة باذن الله تعالي [ḥukiya anna al-afʿā idhā atat ʿalayhā alf sana ʿamiyat wa-qad alhamahā Allāh an tamsaḥ ʿaynayhā bi-waraq al-rāziyānaj al-raṭb fa-yr ilayhā baṣaruhā wa-rubbamā kāna fī barriyya baynahā wa-bayna al-rīf masīrat thalathat ayyām fa-taṭwī tilka al-masāfa ʿalā ṭūlihā wa-ʿalā ʿamāhā ḥattā tuhājim fī baʿḍ al-basātīn ʿalā shajar al-rāziyānaj lā tukhṭīhi fa-taḥukk bihi ʿaynahā fa-tarjiʿ bāṣira bi-idhn Allāh taʿālā] They say that the viper, when it has lived a thousand years, is blinded, and that God inspires it to anoint its eyes with a leaf of fresh fennel, and it recovers its sight. Indeed sometimes it is in the desert, and between it and cultivated land there lies a journey of three days. This distance, however great it is, it traverses, until, having entered some garden, it comes upon a fennel plant, from which it by no means strays, and it rubs its eyes on it, and with God's favour its sight returns to it. Abugiani Thaugidaeus tells a not dissimilar fable: that a kind of serpent is called الشمسية [al-shamsiyya], that is, the Solar, which, when its eyes begin to weaken, turns them toward the sun for the space of an hour on seven successive days, and that by this means its sight is sharpened and strengthened.

They also refer to this the Psalmist's statement that the asp stops its ears against the chant, Psal. LVIII, 7: as though, with a kind of wonderful sagacity, as soon as the asp hears the charmer, it presses one ear to the ground and stops the other with its tail, so that no way lies open to the incantation. But in their place the Arabs will teach us that these words are to be understood quite otherwise.

Consalus Pontius de Leon, in his Notes on the Physiologus of Epiphanius, holds that the serpent's shrewdness consists in the agility of its body. This is what that most ancient Taautus especially praises in the dragon, when, in Eusebius, book 1 of the Praeparatio, he relates that the dragon is πνευματικώτατον τὸ ζῶον πάντων τῶν ἑρπετῶν καὶ πυρῶδες. παρ᾽ ᾧ καὶ τάχος ἀνυπέρβλητον διὰ τοῦ πνεύματος παρίστησι, χωρὶς ποδῶν τε, καὶ χειρῶν, ἢ ἄλλου τινὸς τῶν ἔξωθεν, ἐξ ὧν τὰ λοιπὰ ζῶα τὰς κινήσεις ποιεῖται, καὶ ποικίλων σχημάτων τύπους ἀποτελεῖ, καὶ κατὰ τὴν πορείαν ἑλικοειδεῖς ἔχει τὰς ὁρμὰς, ἐφ᾽ ὃ βούλεται τάχος [pneumatikōtaton to zōon pantōn tōn herpetōn kai pyrōdes. par᾽ hō kai tachos anyperblēton dia tou pneumatos paristēsi, chōris podōn te, kai cheirōn, ē allou tinos tōn exōthen, ex hōn ta loipa zōa tas kinēseis poieitai, kai poikilōn schēmatōn typous apotelei, kai kata tēn poreian helikoeideis echei tas hormas, eph᾽ ho bouletai tachos]: of all reptiles the most spiritual and of a fiery nature; hence it attains extraordinary speed by its breath alone, without the aid of hands or feet or any external organ by which the other animals move; and it shapes itself into various figures, and so, as it goes, it is carried with a winding impetus as swiftly as it pleases. Not far from this opinion is Laurentius Ramirez, in the first chapter of his Pentecontarchus, where he contends that the serpent is called φρόνιμον [phronimon], Gen. III. and Matth. X., for no other reason than that no animal insinuates itself more. From this, he holds, arose the fact that snakes are represented entwined on the caduceus of Mercury, because insinuation is the chief, or nearly the chief, task of the supreme orator, such as Mercury was believed to be. He adds that Eve used to play with the serpent and adorn her bosom, neck and arms with it; and that for this reason necklaces are made even today in the likeness of serpents, which the Greeks [III, 250] call ὄφεις [opheis]. This, besides Nicostratus and Athenaeus, Clement also attests in book 2 of the Paedagogus. But these conjectures of his are too far-fetched to draw me into assent. Especially since I have nowhere read ערמה or φρόνησιν [phronēsin] taken either for agility of body or for insinuation; and, granting that they are so used elsewhere, yet in Christ's words, Be φρόνιμοι [phronimoi], prudent as serpents, and simple as doves, the logic of the antithesis shows that the word φρόνιμοι [phronimoi] must be understood as it sounds. For it is not agility of body or insinuation, but prudence, that is opposed to simplicity. Hence Martial, book 10, Epigr. 47:
— — Prudent simplicity, friends who are equals.

And Paul, Rom. XVI, 9: I would have you wise, that is, prudent, in what is good, and simple in what is evil. Therefore the serpent is truly ערום, that is, φρόνιμος [phronimos], prudent, or πανοῦργος [panourgos], cunning, so far as cunning or prudence can belong to a brute.

This very thing was the reason why the devil used this instrument to seduce man: as though it were more plausible that such crafty counsels should proceed from so crafty an animal, so that Eve might not scent the fraud. But when this had succeeded for Satan as he wished, God cursed not him alone but also the serpent, as the instrument of the seduction. So a judge condemns the forger together with his pen, and the assassin with his weapon. And if anyone has lain with a beast, the divine law orders the beast also to be punished with death, Lev. XX, 15. And God willed a goring ox to be killed together with its owner if it had struck someone through the owner's negligence, Exod. XXI, 28. 29.

Part of the curse is the mutual hatred between the serpent and man: I will put enmity between you and the woman, Gen. III, 15. On account of this hatred Hyperides ^{1)} wrote in his Oration against Demades, τοὺς ὄφεις μισητοὺς εἶναι πάντας [tous opheis misētous einai pantas], that all serpents are worthy of hatred; and Theocritus, Idyll 15:
Ἐκ παιδὸς τὸν ψυχρὸν ὄφιν τὰ μάλιστα δέδοικα [Ek paidos ton psychron ophin ta malista dedoika], From childhood the cold snake has been my horror.

Plautus too, in the Mercator, Act 4: Your wife, of course, is in the country, whom you said a while ago you hated as much as snakes.
